q: Which Linux kernel features provide a container's isolation (what it can see) and resource limits (what it can use)?
options: SELinux for isolation, iptables for limits
Namespaces for isolation, cgroups for resource limits
explain: Namespaces (pid, net, mnt, uts, ipc, user, cgroup) control visibility; cgroups control CPU, memory, PIDs and I/O. Containers share the host kernel; there's no hypervisor per container.

q: In a Node Dockerfile, why do you `COPY package.json package-lock.json ./` and run `npm ci` before `COPY src ./src`?
options: npm requires the lockfile to be in a separate layer
So that code-only changes reuse the cached dependency layer instead of reinstalling every build
explain: Each instruction's cache depends on its inputs. Dependencies change rarely; source changes often. Ordering from least to most frequently changed keeps `npm ci` cached.

q: Which practices make the shipit API runtime image smaller and safer? (select all)
options: Install `curl` and `vim` for debugging in the runtime image
Run as a non-root user with application files owned by root
Compile TypeScript in a build stage and copy only `dist/` and production `node_modules` into the runtime stage
explain: Multi-stage builds, non-root users, read-only code and a tight build context all reduce size and attack surface. Debug tools belong in sidecars or `docker debug`, not the runtime image.

q: Why does the capstone's TypeScript build stage use `FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM`, while the production-dependencies stage doesn't?
options: Compiled JavaScript is architecture-independent, so it can run natively on the builder; production dependencies may contain native code that must match the target platform
Production dependencies can't be cached otherwise
BuildKit requires at least one stage per platform
explain: Running arch-independent work natively avoids slow emulation during multi-platform builds. Anything producing target-specific binaries (native npm modules) must run for the target platform.

q: You mount a named volume at `/var/lib/postgresql/data` on a `postgres:18` container. Data seems to vanish after `docker compose down && up`. Why?
options: Postgres 18 images store data under `/var/lib/postgresql` (version-specific PGDATA) and declare `VOLUME /var/lib/postgresql`, so data went to an anonymous volume
explain: From 18 the image layout changed. Mount at `/var/lib/postgresql` and verify mounts with `docker inspect` after any database change.

q: Inside the api container, which `DATABASE_URL` host is correct when Postgres is the Compose service `db` on the same network, published as `127.0.0.1:15432:5432`?
explain: Container-to-container traffic uses the service name (resolved by Docker's embedded DNS at 127.0.0.11) and the container port. Published host ports are only for access from outside.

q: Which Compose features does the capstone use to start services in the right order? (select all)
options: `depends_on` with `condition: service_completed_successfully` for the migration job
explain: Health-gated dependencies plus a one-off migration job give deterministic startup. `links` is legacy and unnecessary on user-defined networks.

q: In the prod-like stack, `nginx` reaches `api` but cannot reach `db`, and `db` has no internet access. How is that achieved?
options: Two networks: `edge` (web, api) and an `internal: true` `data` network (api, migrate, db, cache)
explain: Services can only resolve and reach peers on shared networks. An internal network has no external gateway. The API is attached to both and bridges the tiers.

q: Where should the DB password live in the prod-like stack?
options: In a Compose secret mounted at `/run/secrets/db_password`, read via `POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE` / `DB_PASSWORD_FILE`
explain: File-based secrets keep the value out of image layers, environment variables and `docker inspect`. In production the file comes from a secret manager.

q: Which runtime settings are applied to `web` and `api` in the prod-like stack? (select all)
explain: These limit what an attacker can do after compromising the process and stop runaway resource use. `privileged` would remove nearly all isolation.

q: A teammate deploys your image to an amd64 server and gets `exec format error`. `docker buildx imagetools inspect` shows only `linux/arm64`. What went wrong?
options: The image was built only for the Mac's native platform; it must be built with `--platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64`
explain: Without `--platform`, buildx builds for the local platform. Multi-arch builds produce an index with one manifest per platform, and each host pulls its own.

q: `docker stop` on the api takes 10 seconds and the exit code is 137. The Dockerfile has `CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]`. What's missing?
options: A SIGTERM handler in the app (Node as PID 1 ignores SIGTERM without one), or `init: true`
explain: As PID 1, Node gets no default SIGTERM action. The capstone's `shutdown()` handler closes the server and pools and exits 0 in well under a second.

q: Why do the capstone's CI and deployment refer to images by digest where possible?
options: A digest is an immutable content hash, so you deploy exactly what you built, scanned and signed; tags can be moved
explain: Tags are mutable pointers. Digest references guarantee immutability, which is the basis for signing, provenance and reproducible deployments.

q: Your Mac's Docker disk is nearly full. Which commands are safe to run without losing your local `shipit_pgdata` database? (select all)
options: `docker volume prune --all` while the stack is down
explain: Build cache, unused images and stopped containers can be recreated. `volume prune --all` removes unused named volumes, including the database when no container references it.
